doc.title: Benny Powell interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, January 16, 1999 [interview 2 of 2]

title: A positive outlook and the kidney illness
summary: Powell explains why he doesn't complain, citing turning bad into good, his Merv Griffin job, and his sister's advice after his kidney trouble.

story.theme_name: Late-career reflections: awards, legacy and life lessons
story.community_name: Life philosophy: faith, karma and how to live

blocks.x: Well it occurs to me that we’ve been talking for about an hour and I have yet to hear you moan and complain about anything.
Oh that’s a luxury I can’t afford.
Well you know, not everybody is like that.

Well I think it would help if they were because I think positive things happen for you only if you think positively, and if you make a bad thing, if you turn a bad thing into a good thing. For instance, like with slavery, maybe if we hadn’t had any slavery we wouldn’t have had a Sarah Vaughan or Billie Holiday and all of that because that’s why I think you can’t wipe out the racial lines. But my point is I guess in my life I’ve taken things — for instance, when I took a job with Merv Griffin, many guys I’m sure said, “Benny Powell is selling out,” or whatever. I’ve had jobs, but I would work with Merv Griffin and get finished with that and go out and play with Thad Jones in the evening. So I guess I, and many people remarked that I came through this kidney dialysis and all of that — in fact Clark Terry calls me King. Now can you imagine that? I just got a message from him, he called and played Happy New Years, but man not in my wildest dreams — Max Roach had some kind of name for me. Now these guys, I came up like a kid, idolizing these guys. Now that’s really because I had a life threatening thing, that has nothing to do with music at all. But that’s what I’m saying. If I had looked at oh woe is me, in fact when it first happened to me I talked to one of my sisters I think when it first happened to me, when I was first inconvenienced by it. My sister said, “I don’t know why it happened to you brother,” but she says, “if you think about what you have as opposed to what you’ve lost, and work with that, I’m sure everything will be fine.” And © Fillius Jazz Archive -24-

at that point I realized how lucky I had been and how lucky I still was. I had something to work with. And I think that if you keep your mind busy, and music is humbling itself, I’m still trying to learn how to play trombone. I have no time to think about I’m sick. I would never have been able to play that way. So have we used up all your tape?
